analysis.one_liner: Makes large factory farms pay for disaster cleanup and animal depopulation and bans the cruelest mass-killing methods.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Agriculture Committee; it sat referred from February 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets the largest industrial farm operators — those running at least 2,500 hogs or 82,000 chickens — and makes them register with a new Agriculture Department office, pay annual disaster-mitigation fees, and cover the full cost of mass animal die-offs, including compensation for neighboring residents. It bans the cheapest mass-killing methods used in past disasters, such as shutting off ventilation so animals overheat to death, and penalizes operators that use them with fines of up to $1,000 per animal. It also gives slaughterhouse and disaster-cleanup workers whistleblower protections, two years of employer-paid health insurance, and 12 weeks of severance, pays contract farmers if their contracts are terminated after a disaster, and rolls back rules that let meat plants run at faster slaughter speeds with fewer federal inspectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Meat and poultry processing workers, who get health coverage, severance, and protection from retaliation; contract farmers, who get lost-revenue payments if an operator cancels their contract after a disaster; people living near large factory farms, who can be compensated for health and property damage; small-scale and higher-welfare farmers, who get grants and inspection support; and food-safety and animal-welfare advocates, since poultry would finally be covered by the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meatplant workers, contract farmers, rural neighbors

how_it_helps.text: Workers doing depopulation work get whistleblower protections, an employer-paid silver-level health plan for at least two years after a disaster event, and 12 weeks of severance if terminated within 60 days after the event.

Contract growers whose contracts are terminated after a disaster must be paid an amount equal to their revenue from the operator over the prior 180 days, and the bill bars operators from cutting wages or grower payments to fund their new fees.

Operators are liable for health impacts, property value losses, and loss of use and enjoyment of property suffered by people living near their facilities, and must fund disposal that does not rely on unlined burial or on-site incineration.

The cheapest mass-killing methods — ventilation shutdown, ventilation shutdown plus, sodium nitrite poisoning, and water-based foaming — are banned, and operators that use them face fines of up to $1,000 per animal and 10-year bans from federal contracts and federal meat inspection.

The bill terminates programs that allow slaughter speeds above existing limits or fewer federal inspectors, funds additional OSHA and meat-inspection inspectors, and makes any person able to sue an operator or USDA over violations, with attorney's fees for prevailing plaintiffs.

The bill's findings state that industrial operators saw a 300-percent growth in profits during the COVID-19 pandemic while more than 60 million poultry and 10 million swine were depopulated since 2019, often with inhumane methods, and that federal support is needed to level the playing field for higher-welfare farmers in a highly monopolized market.

analysis.who_pays: Large industrial farm operators and meat processors pay annual per-animal fees, bear full liability for disaster and depopulation costs, face penalties up to $1,000 per animal for banned killing methods, and lose the deregulated higher-speed slaughter and self-inspection systems they operate under today. Drug makers lose a market for beta-agonist growth drugs. Some of these costs could reach consumers through meat prices.

drawbacks.text: The new fee, liability, and compliance burden falls on large operators, and even with the bill's ban on cutting wages or grower payments to cover fees, some compliance costs could be passed to consumers as higher meat prices.

Cutting the limit on animals in transport from 28 hours to 8 hours, with bedding, water systems, and temperature requirements, would require major changes to livestock hauling fleets; the stricter rule only takes effect ten years after enactment.
Banning beta-agonist drugs such as ractopamine and zilpaterol removes a growth-promotion tool that livestock producers currently use, which could raise production costs.

Bringing poultry under the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act is delayed until ten years after enactment, so poultry slaughter would remain outside that law's protections for a decade even if the bill had passed.

The bill creates a new USDA office, a public database, and a private right of action against operators and the agency itself, which expands federal oversight and litigation exposure that industry groups would argue adds cost without clear benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main gains are worker protections, compensation for surrounding communities, and an end to the worst mass-killing methods, paid for by the companies that caused the problem rather than by taxpayers, who currently absorb disaster cleanup costs. The trade-offs are real: compliance and transport requirements would raise costs for large operators, with some risk those costs reach shoppers, and the poultry slaughter-law fix would not take effect for ten years. On balance the bill shifts costs onto concentrated industry and away from workers, neighbors, and taxpayers, which is why the meat industry would be expected to oppose it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and to two subcommittees, and neither the Agriculture Committee nor any other panel ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James McGovern introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by six original cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the Transportation and Infrastructure and Education and the Workforce Committees.
In early February and March 2023 it was referred to the Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management subcommittee and the Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry subcommittee.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill's action history shows no activity after March 6, 2023, and it expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
All 15 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large industrial farm operators and meat processors are better off because the bill died: they keep the current rules that let them run faster slaughter lines with fewer federal inspectors, avoid annual fees and full liability for disaster and depopulation costs, and remain free to use ventilation-shutdown killing methods without penalty. Taxpayers also continue to share the cost of cleanup when mass die-offs occur.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill; with a Republican majority controlling the House calendar, it never advanced.

industries.industry: Industrial livestock and poultry operators (large factory farms)
industries.note: They would pay annual per-animal fees, bear full liability for disaster and depopulation costs including harm to neighbors, face fines up to $1,000 per animal and 10-year bans for using ventilation shutdown and similar methods, and register plans publicly. Their current model, which externalizes disaster costs to taxpayers, workers, and neighbors, would be priced at its true cost.

The bill terminates the higher-speed slaughter and self-inspection systems these plants operate under and funds more OSHA and federal meat inspectors. It partially offsets that with $750 million in voluntary grants to switch to gas stunning, but only for facilities that sign labor peace agreements with unions and stay independent of large packers.

Growers would receive lost-revenue payments if operators cancel their contracts after disasters, and workers doing depopulation work would get health coverage, severance, and whistleblower protection paid by the operators.
The bill bans using ractopamine, zilpaterol, and lubabegron for growth promotion or feed efficiency, eliminating a drug market tied to livestock becoming unable to stand.

industries.industry: Small-scale, mobile, and higher-welfare processors and farmers
industries.note: They would receive a $50 million pilot program for expanded inspection access, prioritized inspector hiring, and support in disaster plans that directs operators to contract with small-scale processors. The bill's findings call this a way to level the playing field against monopolized industrial operators.
